en: Preface to the *Xùjì* (Explanatory Record) of the *Kēfǎ Yíngqūshè Sòngshū* (Commentary on the Verses of the Abhidharmakośa): There was once a person who climbed a certain mountain to gaze upon its heights;

treading over rugged precipices and parting the thickets and brambles, he sought to reach its most remote and magnificent summit to explore the dens of tigers and leopards and tread where dragons and serpents dwell, until his strength was utterly exhausted.
Limping and staggering, he was ultimately unable to proceed and returned home.

Thereafter, when we gathered again with our hairpins tucked up and remained in a state of lingering revelry, someone boasted of the supreme excellence of that peak. I felt much resentment and an overwhelming sense of regret in my breast, saying:
"If I do not go there again to explore and uncover its wonders, it shall be as I have sworn. Thus it has been said by others.
I traveled to such-and-such a mountain, inhaling the azure mist from its tiered peaks and clutching at flying creepers on its winding ridges.

My breath was short and my mouth agape, making a sound like that of sawing wood; yet when I reached what were called its most extraordinary sights, my bones would shiver and my fingers bite into my flesh, as if my very life were being weighed against them.
Upon returning, however, I remained exhausted for three days; even a distance of a few feet outside my door required me to stand on tiptoe to reach it.
When Chu Yue recalls its extraordinary and sublime beauty, it compensates for his weariness; yet those who have actually heard of it are perhaps very few.
Now, among the scholars of this world who study the classical texts, those who are like people ascending a peak to gaze upon the vista are not few.
As for the preface to the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā-bhāṣya-ṭīkā* by Master Faying, its citations, explanations, and comprehensive summaries [serve as such a guide].

The detailed analysis of the authentic teachings is revered among scholars within the academies; it differs vastly from what is currently called the "wooden disaster" (a term for superficial or distorted interpretations).
As for those who have not yet taken up these texts in their book-cases, will they not feel the same regret as one who has ascended a certain mountain but cannot reach its sublime heights?
Nevertheless, when one studies and contemplates them, one must rely upon and cite [the authentic sources].
Yet there are those who are hesitant and cautious, like one who, startled by a physician’s exhaustive search for a poison arrow in a dying man, unravels it with trepidation;
or like one who is hesitant and wavering, like an inferior steed attempting to mate with a stallion.

In sum, these are what are called those who have an abundance of antiquarian research but a deficiency in illuminating insight. Those who seek to trace and unravel [the meaning] should likewise not be without such [caution].
When people travel to the sublime wonders of a certain mountain and return, they harbor regrets; thus, there was formerly no record of this, but now it is being inscribed.

However, this present inscription is intended solely for those who, like one pointing toward the sun or shooting an arrow, plan to visit again, rather than for those who, like one lying down in a single room, find Chu and Yue to be but a few inches apart.

The *Kārikā* is what is called the "Verses," and the *Bhāṣya* is its commentary on the *Abhidharmakośa*; since these two have already become separated, how much more so the case of the minor fragments—the preface to the *Kārikā* and the records?
Is this not like one who has learned to swim only to drown again? For this reason, I have not yet ventured to plan [the publication].
On a day in the ninth month of autumn in the Guiwei year of the Genroku era,
the śramaṇa Daokong composed this preface to the *Commentary on the Verses of the Abhidharmakośa*. Revised by the śramaṇa Faying of Jian’an.
Explanation of the preceding introduction is divided into two parts: first, praising the benefit of the emergence of the treatise in the Western Land;

second, from "The Tripitaka Master of the Great Tang" onwards, the reasons for requesting the compilation of a commentary upon its transmission and translation here in this land. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, praising the capacity for the thousand works; second, from "As for...
onwards, specifically manifesting the virtues of this particular treatise. "In the past, Śākyamuni... to the thousand works" is the general heading for the thousand works.
Regarding the phrase "In the past" (*sīzé*) from the *Yì*: it means that when the sages created the *Yì*, they took the past and the present as "the past" (*sī*).

Śākyamuni is his clan name; this is translated as "Capable Benevolence" (*Néngrén*). Long ago, at the beginning of the Bhadrakalpa, there was a king named Samata (translated as Gòngxǔ, "Universally Honored");
he was of the Kṣatriya caste and was a distant ancestor of the Buddha. This prince’s descendants have maintained the lineage in succession.

The nineteenth Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) was named Mahāmeru. His descendants succeeded one another for one hundred seventy-three thousand two hundred eighty-four minor Universal Monarchs; the last of these Universal Monarchs was named Matsyaputra.
His descendants succeeded one another for one hundred forty-three minor regional kings (Kṣudraka-rāja); the last of these kings was named...

The Great King of Maoshu was the seventh-generation ancestor of the Buddha. Having initially been childless, he entrusted the affairs of state to his ministers and entered the mountains to practice the Way.
There, he was accidentally shot by a hunter and passed away; as his flesh fell, drops of blood struck the ground and produced two stalks of sugarcane.
A noble spirit destined for sovereignty had secretly taken refuge within the sugarcane; when it was opened and sliced by the sun’s heat, one stalk emerged.
A son was born named Sujāta, and a daughter was born named Bhaddā. The ministers immediately installed Sujāta as the successor to the throne;
from this time on, he was known as the Gautama clan—this being translated as the "Sun-burnt" lineage or the "Sugarcane" lineage—which is the sixth-generation ancestor of the Buddha.
Later, due to the jealousy of the principal queen, she subsequently banished the four brothers, including the half-brother Nigrodha.

This is called "Separately Established" (Videha), etc. Because the four sons who settled in the Snowy Mountains established kingdoms and brought peace to the people, when the father-king heard this, he praised them, saying:
"My sons are capable and benevolent; my sons are capable and benevolent. For this reason, they established the clan name Śākya. This was the fifth generation ancestor of the Buddha.
If one speaks of Gautama or Gotama, these are mostly terms used by non-Buddhists to disparage the Buddha. Vasubandhu Bodhisattva...
"Sā" (Sa) is *devapandita* in Sanskrit, which means "Heavenly Relative" (*Tianqin*) in Chinese; both the Chinese and Sanskrit forms are corruptions.
The old transcription was *Vasupandita*, while the new transcription is *Vasubandhu*, also written as *Vasu-paṇḍu*; this means "Worldly Relative.
At the beginning of the eon, the Lord of Sovereignty (*Īśvara*) manifested twenty-four times in the human realm to propagate the teachings, and on his twenty-fourth manifestation, he appeared.
The three-eyed, eight-armed deity encountered the Mūkapāda ṛṣi, who said to the ṛṣi, "If there are three eyes upon my face, then you may debate with me.
The ṛṣi lifted his foot and replied, "If there were eyes beneath my feet, then I would debate with you.
The deity knew he had fallen into defeat; he manifested a gaunt and emaciated form and returned to his original heaven, never to appear again.
When he came to the human realm, people admired his celestial virtue and established a shrine for him, casting his body in gold and his eyes in crystal.
His pedestal was twenty feet high, and this celestial image was called Vāsavadatta; because he acted as a close friend to the people of the world, he was known as Lokeśvara (World-Kinsman).
From the celestial shrine, he requested three sons, all of whom were obtained from the very places they were sought.
Regarding the name: In the region of North India there is a country named Puruṣapura. *Puruṣa* means "man" (*zhàngfū*) and *pura* means "city" (*zhì*).
This country was established by the younger brother of Śakra, who was able to subdue the asuras and establish a manly resolve;
it was for this reason that the name was given. According to the *Vaiśravaṇadevarāja-āgama*, Śakra dispatched his younger brother to subdue the asuras.
The deva Viśvānu was born in this country as Prince Devaputra. In this country there is an asura named Indradamaya;
"Indra" is the name for Śakra, and "damaya" means "to subdue.
This asura possesses great power and constantly battles with Śakra; because he is able to subdue Śakra, he has this name. There is an asura... [text ends]
The sister’s name was Bhābhāvatī; *bhā* means "light" and *bhāvatī* means "queen.

Because the asuras wished to harm Viṣṇu, they took this sister and, by the power of incantations, transformed a region of Jambudvīpa into darkness so that they might dwell there in concealment, unseen by others.
They then spoke to their sister from within the dark place, directing her toward the light.
The sister said, "If there is anyone who wishes to take you as his wife, tell him: 'My brother possesses great power;
if he takes me as his wife, he will surely come into conflict with my brother. Only if you can fight against my brother may I grant my consent.
Later, when Viṣṇu saw her heart’s great joy, he asked, "Who are you? She replied, "I am an Asura."
The maiden goddess said, "Asuras vomit up their brides for the sake of the various devas; I have no wife, and you have no husband—let us take one another.

The girl replied as her elder brother had previously instructed: "The deva said, 'If it is because you love me that you speak these words, I possess great power and can fight against your elder brother.
He then granted his consent. The asura went to the place of light and asked the goddess, "Who are you?"
The man said, "I have already taken your sister as my wife. The Asura replied, "I am no man; you may hold me to this reproach.
Prove that I am a man, and why do you now find fault with me? The Asura asked, "What ability do you possess to claim for yourself the title of 'man'?
If you can defeat me in battle, then you may take your sister as your wife. The man said, "Let us then decide it. Immediately, each took up a sword and a spear, and they attacked one another.
They struck and stabbed one another with the strength of Nārāyaṇa; though they hacked and pierced the celestial body, no wound could penetrate it.
When the devas hacked at the limbs and members of the asuras, they were severed only to grow back again, continuing until evening without ceasing. There was no sign of death among them.

As the celestial power gradually weakened and the pratyekabuddhas grew exhausted, the asuras' strength increased further into the night. Fearing that the devas would not prevail, the vidyārājñī [the Bright Consort] immediately—
He took an *urubra* flower, split it into two pieces, and threw each to one side;
as he moved away from between them and returned, the deva understood his intent and seized the asura’s body, splitting it into two pieces and throwing each to one side;
as he moved away from between them and returned, the asura died. Previously, while at the abode of the rishi, he had made a vow, saying: "If..."
When my hands, feet, and limbs were severed, they immediately grew back; for this reason I did not die.

The *ṛṣi* wished to have me killed by the devas, but because I made no offering and restored my body, he caused my death through his vow. The devas dwell in this land to manifest the resolve of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*).
One can establish a reputation based on this as a "Great Man's Resolve Country. In this land, there is a state preceptor who is a *brāhmaṇa*.
The gatekeeper was named Kauśika and had three sons, collectively known as Vāsava.
They obtained their names from the celestial realm of the Lord of Heaven (Indra), taking the names of the divine chapels there. His third son was Pilindavatsa;
Pilindi was the mother’s name, which translates as "child" or "son. He left the household life to join the Sarvāstivāda school and attained the fruit of Arhatship.
The second son then took the collective name [of his lineage] and entered the order in the Sarvāstivāda school.

He was profoundly learned and widely erudite, thoroughly mastering the classical scriptures and composing numerous treatises. His most significant work is titled *Asaṅga* (translated here as "Non-attachment").

He also entered the order in the Mahīśāsaka school—or it is said he did so in the Sarvāstivāda—where he cultivated meditative concentration, became free from desire, and attained the Mahāyāna contemplation of emptiness; for this reason, he received this title.
It is said that Asaṅga’s younger brother, Vasubandhu, while lecturing on the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* in the kingdom of Gandhāra, had completed six hundred stanzas of verse.

Holding the Hīnayāna to be the truth and disbelieving that the Mahāyāna was the Buddha’s teaching, Asaṅga—seeing that his brother’s intelligence surpassed his own and fearing he would disparage the Mahāyāna treatises and fall into the evil realms—sent a messenger to inform him: "I am now ill; you should come quickly."
Vasubandhu followed his brother to a monastery forty *li* away. There, he heard a disciple of Asaṅga reciting the "Ten Stages" chapter (*Daśabhūmika*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

He was moved to a profound realization and felt deep remorse, thinking: "How marvelous and subtle is this Dharma, which I have never heard before! Only now do I realize that the Lesser Vehicle was mistaken.
He understood that the source of the transgression of slandering the Dharma originated in the tongue; thus, the tongue is the root of all sin.
"Now it is fitting that you sever [this attachment] immediately. He then took up a sharp blade, intending to cut out his own tongue to atone for his offense.

Just as he was about to do so, he saw Wuzhu standing before him, who addressed him, saying: "The Mahāyāna teachings are the principle of ultimate truth; they are praised by all Buddhas and revered by the multitude of sages.
I intended to instruct you, yet you have now awakened to this yourself. To awaken to such clarity—what could be more auspicious? It is just as [the sūtras say]..."
"In the holy teaching of the Buddha, cutting out one's tongue is not considered repentance; even if you were to have your tongue cut off, it would not extinguish your prior transgression.
Since you have incurred this sin by slandering the Mahāyāna Dharma because of your tongue, if you wish to extinguish it, you must skillfully praise and expound the Mahāyāna.

For the Mahāyāna can naturally remedy such faults and cause this sin to be swiftly extinguished. As for your claim that 'closing one's mouth and ceasing to speak' is the proper principle—where does such a logic reside? Having spoken these words, he...
Suddenly, he was no longer seen in the world; Vasubandhu received his command and consequently refrained from cutting out his tongue.

He then went to the residence of Asaṅga to inquire about and receive the Mahāyāna teachings. Thereupon, he applied himself with refined diligence and profound reflection, composing five hundred Mahāyāna treatises to explain the Mahāyāna sūtras.
At the age of eighty, he passed away in the kingdom of Aśmaka. Although his traces remained within the realm of ordinary beings, his reality was truly inconceivable.
"Compilation" (*zhuǎn*) means to collect. For example, the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors possessed both virtue and rank, so they established institutions and authored works;

Confucius possessed virtue but lacked such rank, so he transmitted rather than composed. Now, it is said that the Buddha has already expounded the expositions on principles and the treatises on doctrine within the other two *piṭakas*.
This treatise master has now compiled them in one place, and thus it is called "The Compendium of a Thousand Treatises. To propagate [this work]...
"To proclaim far and wide" means that the Dharma-sound of the Buddha’s Way is propagated upward and its influence spreads afar; this is due to one's resolve.

It refers to the extensive propagation and thorough elucidation of the Tathāgata’s scriptures, reaching as far as the vast reaches of the trichiliocosm in space and spanning twelve thousand years in time.
"To initiate much that is excellent" refers to the downward transformation of sentient beings; "excellent" (*liáng*) means wholesome. It means to initiate wholesome faith.
"Many" (*zhě duō*) means that the meaning and principles are manifested through the treatises and teachings;

sentient beings, by means of the wisdom acquired at birth (*upapattipratilambhikā prajñā*), are able to generate the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and so forth through the study of these treatises and teachings—thus "many" refers to this manifestation of understanding. To speak broadly of the merit of the treatises and teachings, it does not go beyond two things:
above, propagating the Buddha-way, and below, transforming sentient beings; therefore, these two matters are cited. Ximing quotes the *Analects*: [the passage follows].
Xia asked: "What is meant by 'The clever smile is radiant; the beautiful eyes are bright; with plainness as the ground for the embroidery'? " The commentary explains:
This is Xia questioning the meaning of a passage from the *Shi Jing*. The first two lines are from the second chapter of the "Shuo Ren" (Describing the Lady) in the *Wei Feng* (Air of Wei).
Qi Hou's daughter, Zhuang Jiang, was the wife of Duke Zhuang of Wei. Duke Zhuang was infatuated with his favorite concubine and allowed her to treat the [Dowager] with arrogance.

[The Duke of] Zeng [was] virtuous like Lady Zhuang, yet she received no response from him; in the end, she remained childless. The people of the state pitied her and grieved for her, and thus composed this poem.
The commentary states: *qiàn* (third tone) refers to beautiful lips and cheeks; *mù xiàn* (to gaze with wide eyes) means the black and white of the eyes are clearly distinguished.

The *Shāngshū Zhǔjì* states: "This chapter describes the beauty of Lady Zhuang’s countenance. The *Lúnyǔ Zhù* by Mǎ [Wáng] says: "*qiàn* is the appearance of a beautiful smile; *xiàn* is the movement of the eyes."
"The appearance is plain, yet it is made brilliant by the white underneath"—this one line is missing. It was lost because the books were burned during the Qin dynasty;
thus, it is not included in the *Shi* (Book of Poetry). The Master said, "In painting, the white comes after. Zheng’s commentary states: "Painting" refers to decorative patterns.
In all painting, one first applies various colors and then uses the white to be distributed among them to complete the pattern; this serves as a metaphor.
"Though the Lady Jiang possesses a beautiful and alluring nature, she must still be completed by means of ritual. He said, "Is it not ritual that comes after? The commentary states:

When Zixia heard that "painting is followed by the white ground," he interpreted this by using the white ground as a metaphor for ritual; thus he asked, "Is it not ritual that comes after? The Master said, "Shang has inspired me!
From now on, you may truly be said to understand the *Shi*. The commentary explains that Zixia was able to bring forth [the deeper meaning].

The Master’s intention was that [Yan] Shang could be consulted regarding the recitation of the *Shi* (Odes), let alone discussing the master’s composition of this treatise, which re-initiates the teachings of the Sūtras and Vinaya.

However, to employ such an approach for its propagation would be a far-reaching interpretation; as the meaning is already established, it is not adopted here. (The above is a general praise of the thousandfold treatises.

Below, the specific significance of this treatise is revealed. [The character] Jié (pronounced *qùjié*, meaning "to raise high"; according to the *Sāncāng*, it means "to lift," "to carry," or "to bear") signifies solemnity.
The Master said: "To 'reveal' (jie) means to walk with the sun and moon [held high]; it is also said that one 'carries a sack, reveals a chest, and bears a casket while hurrying.

In all these cases, the term is glossed as 'to lift up' (ju). To 'analyze' (pou; pǔ hòu fǎn; meaning 'to divide') names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*) means that 'names' are the designating terms for all phenomena, while 'characteristics' are the essential bodies or the formal appearances of those phenomena.
This treatise consists of approximately thirty fascicles; its subject matter is vast and its scope extensive."

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* and other treatises by Vasubandhu and others encompass, from a distance, the matters contained within the ninefold scriptures (*navāṅga-dharma*) and the Vinaya spoken by the Buddha during the first forty years of his ministry.

"Skillful" (*gong*) means clever or adept. This refers to the fact that those who can thoroughly investigate the principles of the faculties (*indriya*) and the elements (*dhātu*) are universally praised for the skillfulness of this treatise.
From here on, the text specifically describes how this treatise is capable of investigating the roots—that is, the faculties.
This chapter clarifies the functions of all phenomena; the "Chapter on Elements" (Dhātu-paṭala) clarifies the essence and intent of all phenomena.
Those who exhaustively investigate the source of worldly sages—these two chapters clarify the causes and effects of the mundane and supramundane.

In taking up practice and exertion to move from cause toward effect, nothing surpasses these. To distinguish cause and effect within the ultimate and conventional truths is to explain the aforementioned [nature of] worldly sages.

The "Chapter on Karma" (*Karmavarga*) clarifies the causes of conventional truth; the "Chapter on Latent Tendencies" (*Anuśayavarga*) clarifies the conditions of conventional truth; the "Chapter on Knowledge" (*Jñānavarga*) clarifies the causes of ultimate truth;

and the "Chapter on Meditative Concentration" (*Samādhivarga*) clarifies the conditions of ultimate truth. "Dispelling attachment to the self and persons" (*pudgala-ātma-abhiniveśa-vinodana*): "dispelling" (*vinodana*) means to remove or eliminate.

This explains the principle of investigating the sense bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*); these two chapters distinguish the three categories of the Dharma-gate (*triskandha-dharmamukha*) to eliminate the grasping at a self.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "having already reflected upon more than half" (*sī yǐ guò bàn*): the *Appended Statements* (Xìcí) of the lower section of the *Zhou Yī* states, "The wise man observes its *tuàn* (hexagram judgment) and has already reflected upon more than half [of the meaning].
The commentary notes: "Now, the *tuàn* summarizes the general principles of the three images. Furthermore, the *Lüèlì* (Brief Examples) asks: "What is the *tuàn*?
It is that which comprehensively discusses the structure of a single hexagram and clarifies the primary line from which it proceeds. This refers to Fuxi’s drawing of the eight trigrams.
The hexagrams were further doubled to form the sixty-four hexagrams. Subsequently, King Wen composed the lines of text beneath each hexagram, which are called the *tuan* (彖) commentaries;
for example, the passage under the Qian hexagram stating "Great success, benefit, perseverance, and correctness" (*yuan heng li zhen*) is such a commentary. *Tuan* means to judge or determine;
it determines the structure of a hexagram and the meaning of its good or ill fortune. It is also called the *zhao* (繇) commentary. *Zhao* means to extract; it extracts the essence of a single...
This is the general purport of the hexagrams. Later, the Duke of Zhou further expounded the words for the six lines (*yao*).

Since these are the words beneath the lines—such as "The first nine of Qian: the hidden dragon; do not act"—they are called *yao-ci* (line-words). It was only with Confucius that the Ten Wings (*Shi Yi*) were created:
1. Upper *Tuan* (Judgment), 2. Lower *Tuan*, 3. Upper *Xiang* (Image), 4. Lower *Xiang*, 5. Upper *Xici* (Appended Statements), 6. Lower *Xici*, and 7. Wenyan... [text truncated].
Regarding the eight *Shuogua*, nine *Xugua*, and ten *Zagua*: this treatise resembles the *Tuan* commentaries of the *Yijing* and the *Vinaya*.
Among the twelve divisions of the scriptures, it clarifies more than half of the names of the first nine divisions.

As for those who specialize in attacking the teaching of "existence" (*you*) alone—"attack" here meaning to strike down—it does not merely clarify the teaching of existence in the Hīnayāna, but also contains the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) in the Mahāyāna.
Alternatively, it may be that not only the Sarvāstivāda school is discussed, but also the doctrines of various schools such as the Sautrāntika.

From here below is the second section, "The Transmission and Translation in This Land," which is divided into two parts: first, the translation of the treatise; second, the request to compose a commentary.

The Tripitaka Master of the Great Tang was surnamed Chen and was a native of Yanshi County in the Eastern Capital (Luoyang). In the second year of the Zhenguan era, he traveled to the Five Indias, and by the tenth...
In the first month of the ninth year, he arrived in Chang’an with six hundred and fifty-seven Sanskrit texts, among which was the *Abhidharmakośa*.
On the sixth day of the second month, by imperial decree, he began the translation at Hongfu Monastery. This was a re-translation of the authentic text;

the version translated during the Chen dynasty is considered the first, while that translated during the Tang dynasty is the second. The principles elucidated therein are correct, and the phrasing is definitive.

Regarding the True Text: those who personally received his secret instructions include the various masters of the Mahāyāna in the Western Regions (India) from whom the Tripiṭaka Master received the oral transmission of both establishment and refutation, and he bestowed the meaning of the Hīnayāna upon Dharma Master Ji;
furthermore, there were such figures as Dharma Master Guṇamati, who rescued the principles of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.
Second, following this, is the request to compose the commentary (*śāstra*). As for the "correct explanation," the thirty fascicles constitute the correct explanation itself.

Regarding the statement that [the music] is both "exhaustively beautiful" (*jin mei*) and "exhaustively good" (*jin shan*), the *Lunyu* says: "The Master said, 'As for the *Shao*, it is exhaustively beautiful and also exhaustively good;
as for the *Wu*, it is exhaustively beautiful but not exhaustively good. *Shao* is the name of the music of Shun. Now, when sages compose music, they give it names according to the human mind.
*Shao* means 'to continue' (*shao*); because Shun succeeded to Yao's virtue through the ritual of yielding, he accordingly composed [this music]."
"Beautiful" (*mei*) refers to that which is capable of harmonizing with the appellation of the time; "good" (*shan*) refers to the name of one whose affairs and principles are not flawed.
When the myriad people of the world rejoiced that Shun succeeded Yao, and Shun accepted the abdication from the people, this accorded with the hearts of the age;

therefore, it is said to be "utterly beautiful. As for the yielding through ritual bows and replacing [the throne], the principles of affairs reached their ultimate purpose; therefore, it is said to be "utterly good."
As for the *Wu* (The Martial), it is the name of the music of King Wu. At that time, Zhou of Yin had practiced evil for a long duration, and the myriad people were resentful and enraged.
King Wu launched his military expeditions; by exercising martial power, he brought peace to the hearts of the world, and thus the music was named "The Martial.

The world delighted in King Wu’s martiality. King Wu followed the will of the people to strike down Zhou; this accorded with the hearts of the age, and therefore it was "perfectly beautiful" (*jin mei*). This was because of his ministers.
Regarding the phrase "the ruler was attacked": because there was no goodness in the administration of affairs, it is said that "goodness was not yet exhausted. Now, as for the intent of this preface:

when the Tripiṭaka was first transmitted and translated, Dharma Master Guang received secret instructions and composed a commentary (*śāstra*) to explain it, exhausting the propriety of both principle and phenomena.
What more could be added to this? Why, then, do you further request the composition of another commentary? As for the names of the music of the Three Augusts, Five Emperors, and Three Kings:
Since antiquity, there have been the lineages of Tianhuang, Dihuang, and Renhuang; the records of fifty clans, seventy-two clans, three clans, six clans, and four clans.
From the time of Youcaoshi and Suirenshi onwards, there were none who possessed ritual and music. The common people inhaled the essence of the dew and ate the fruits of plants and trees;
those who lived in the mountains subsisted on insufficient food, while those dwelling by the water fed upon birds and beasts.
Those people ate fish and turtles, drank blood, and wore raw fur and skins; many suffered from injuries and illnesses.

It was only with the advent of Sui Ren that he began drilling wood for fire-tapers to produce fire, teaching people to smelt gold to make cauldrons and tripods so they might cook their food before eating it;
thus he was titled Sui Ren, and the Five Elements were thereby brought forth. When Fu Xi, the Great Hao, subsequently ruled as a sovereign of the Wood Virtue, he first established the Eight Trigrams.
The hexagrams were used to communicate with the spiritual intelligences; the rites of marriage were established, and the music of the *qin* and *se* was first created.

Under the Lord of Shenong, the Emperor of Fire, auspicious grain grew and sweet springs gushed forth; he compiled the *Bencao*, fashioned the five-stringed *qin*, and composed the music of "Non-deliberate Planning.
Under Youxiong, the Yellow Emperor—whose surname was Gongsun and whose name was Xuanyuan—he composed the music of *Yunmen* and *Xianchi*. [Under] Jintian...
Shi Xiaohao composed the music of Nine Springs; Gaoyang Shizhuanxu composed the music of Receiving the Clouds.
It is further said that he employed Flying Dragons to release the sounds of the Eight Winds and composed the music of Five Splendors.
